summary.text: Stratified sampling splits a population into subgroups called strata, then samples within each subgroup separately.
Every member of the population must belong to one and only one stratum, and the sampling inside each stratum can be simple random sampling.
Its aim is to improve precision by reducing sampling error, and it is generally used when the population is not a uniform group.

facts.label: Strata rule
facts.value: Every member is assigned to one and only one stratum

facts.label: Main goal
facts.value: Improve precision by reducing sampling error

facts.label: Proportionate allocation
facts.value: Each stratum's sampling fraction matches its share of the population

facts.label: Optimum allocation
facts.value: Larger samples go to the strata with the greatest variability

items.prompt: A country has three towns of 1, 2 and 3 million people, filled with factory workers, office workers and retirees. A pollster can ask 60 people about an election. Which plan gives a smaller error?

options.label: Ask 60 people drawn at random from the whole country
Ask 10, 20 and 30 people from the three towns in turn
Ask all 60 people in the smallest town
Ask all 60 people in the largest town

items.explain: A purely random sample of 60 might be poorly balanced across the towns, while sampling each town in proportion gives a smaller error for the same total size.

items.prompt: A researcher splits people into "under 40" and "has a job" and plans to sample each group. What is wrong with these groups?

options.label: Some people fit both groups and others fit neither
The two groups must always be exactly the same size
Groups should be formed only after sampling is done
Splitting a population into groups is never allowed

items.explain: Strata should be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, so each member belongs to one and only one stratum.

items.prompt: When does splitting a population into strata give a smaller error in the estimate?

options.label: When all the groups have exactly the same size
When each group is as varied as the whole population
When people within each group are more alike than the whole population is
When the groups overlap so that nobody is missed

items.explain: If measurements within strata have a lower standard deviation than the population overall, stratification gives a smaller error in estimation.

items.prompt: A survey of a whole province has a sparsely populated north and a crowded south. Why might it sample a larger share of people in the north?

options.label: Northern residents are always harder to reach by phone
Northern opinions matter more than southern opinions
The south is already too well studied to include
A province-wide share would yield only a handful of northern answers

items.explain: Because north and south differ so much in population, one sampling fraction for the whole province could collect only a handful of data from the north.

items.prompt: A club has 60 men and 40 women. Using proportionate allocation, how many women belong in a sample of 10?
items.explain: Proportionate allocation makes each stratum's share of the sample match its share of the population, and women are 40 of 100 people.

items.prompt: Optimum allocation splits a fixed sample between two equal-sized strata, one with very erratic values and one with nearly identical values. Where does the bigger share go?

options.label: The steady stratum, because it is easy to measure
The erratic stratum, to keep overall sampling variance lowest
Equally to both, so neither feels neglected
Whichever stratum happens to have more data on hand

items.explain: Larger samples are taken in the strata with the greatest variability to generate the least possible overall sampling variance.
